newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says budget will not hit the poor.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says budget will not hit the poor.

text.p: Italian prime minister Romano Prodi, facing opposition from key hard-left allies over proposed income tax modifications, said on Sunday that his centre-left government would not hit the poor in the 1997 budget.
Prodi, in Florence for a conference, insisted that the effect of proposed tax rises for lower earners would be compensated by allowances and deductions.
"The revision of tax bands will be accompanied by a major reform of deductions," Prodi said.
"The lowest earners will not be worse off under this budget, while the poorest section will not pay taxes, as before.
"It would be unthinkable that my government could start out with a financial injustice of this sort," he said.

Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, whose party holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, criticised the plans at the weekend in comments widely seen as threatening the budget's passage.
"It's not good enough. The government is running the risk of compromising its rapport with the country," Bertinotti was quoted as saying by Italian newspapers.
He added that "too many choices appear unplanned and do not in any case reflect the common will of the majority."
The Rome daily Il Messaggero quoted him as saying "we will never vote for this amendment."
Prodi suggested the uproar over taxation was due mainly to a lack of information and precise figures. "Everything will be cleared up when the figures are looked at," he said.
"The finance minister has already clarified the general aspects. Now, figures in hand, we will see that the alarm is not justified."

The finance ministry has said it plans to introduce a new regional tax aimed at corporates and self-employed workers as well as an increase in personal income tax, with money from this going back to the regions.
The government, facing strong federalist demands from northern Italy, has pledged to increase the fiscal power of the regions in a bid to cut the influence of central administration.

It last month unveiled an austerity budget designed to swipe 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit -- double the size of the originally planned package. The budget must be approved by the end of the year.
